content.title: And the Qur'an Was Being Revealed Among Them: When the Events of Makkah Became Verses Recited
paragraphs: Chapter Fourteen — And the Qur'an Was Being Revealed Among Them: When the Events of Makkah Became Verses Recited

The previous chapters described Muslims being tortured in Makkah, men of Quraysh arguing with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, others mocking the Qur’an, and leading men demanding that vulnerable believers be excluded from his gathering so they could sit with him separately. These events form only part of the picture. The Qur’an was being revealed in their midst, not years later simply to recount them. An incident, an objection, or a trial could be followed by verses strengthening the Prophet and his Companions, answering an opponent, or exposing the motives behind a position. Reading the Seerah therefore helps us understand some verses, while the Qur’an reveals aspects of the Seerah that historical reports alone may not show.

Understanding this relationship requires distinctions between kinds of evidence. Some verses are connected to an event by an authentic hadith identifying what happened and who spoke. Elsewhere, commentators cite reports about the circumstances of revelation, but those reports vary in reliability. A third kind of connection is an interpretation drawn from the text and its context: a commentator sees how a verse addresses the Prophet’s situation without claiming an explicit report that it was revealed because of that event. This chapter keeps those distinctions clear.
Do people think once they say, “We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test?

After seeing Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, on the scorching ground of Makkah, and seeing what happened to the family of Yasir and other vulnerable believers, the opening of Surat al-'Ankabut becomes much closer to the reality of those years:

Alif Lām Mīm.
Do people think once they say, “We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test?
We certainly tested those who came before them. For Allah will surely make known those who are truthful and those who are liars.
— Qur’an 29:1–3 — Rowwad Translation Center

Being tested here means facing trials and hardships through which steadfastness in faith becomes evident. The wording is general: professing faith does not guarantee a life without trials. Al-Tabari also transmits a report connecting these verses to the torture of Muslims, including ‘Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him. That report does not limit the verse’s meaning, but illustrates the circumstances in which the believers were hearing the Qur’an.
The believers heard Allah’s words:
Do people think once they say, “We believe,” that they will be left without being put to the test?
They heard these words in a society where they were not secure from harm. Some knew believers being beaten and tortured for their faith; some may have suffered themselves.
The Nobles of Quraysh and Sitting with the Vulnerable Believers

The conflict also concerned who sat around the Prophet ﷺ, not only what he said. Tribe, lineage, and wealth strongly influenced social standing in Makkah. Yet among his Companions were men with little wealth and no powerful tribal protection, including Bilal, Khabbab, and Suhayb, may Allah be pleased with them.

Reports in Qur'anic commentary mention that some of the leading men of Quraysh wanted the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to send these weaker believers away from his gathering so that the elite could sit with him apart from them. Sahih Muslim also records Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, saying that the verse concerned six Companions, including himself and Ibn Mas‘ud, after the polytheists objected to their being kept close to the Prophet ﷺ.
Then Allah revealed:

Do not send away [O Prophet] those who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face [pleasure]. You are not accountable for them whatsoever, nor are they accountable for you whatsoever. If you still send them away, you will be one of the wrongdoers.
— Qur’an 6:52 — Rowwad Translation Center
“Morning and evening” refers to the beginning and end of the day.
The same meaning appears again in Allah's words:

Be patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not turn your eyes away from them, desiring the adornments of the life of this world.
— Qur’an 18:28 — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

Do not turn your eyes away from them, desiring the adornments of the life of this world.
The instruction is not to shift attention away from these believers toward others.

The message was not to win the approval of the powerful by excluding vulnerable believers. The Qur’an established that a person’s worth before Allah is not measured by tribe, wealth, or status in Makkah. Several people whom the Qurayshi elite considered beneath their company would become among the best-known Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Even the Number of the Angels of Hell Became a Subject of Mockery
Confrontation took the form of mockery as well as torture and boycott. Allah says of Hell:

It is overseen by nineteen [angels].
— Qur’an 74:30 — Rowwad Translation Center
That is, nineteen angels are appointed over it.

Reports in Qur’anic commentary mention that when Abu Jahl heard the number, he treated it as though it referred to nineteen human men whom Quraysh might fight. They describe him mockingly asking his people whether every ten of them would be unable to overcome one of the keepers of the Fire.
The following verse clarifies:

We have only appointed angels as keepers of the Fire, and We have only made their number as a test for the disbelievers, […]
— Qur’an 74:31 — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)

The keepers of the Fire are the angels appointed over it. The accounts of this mockery appear in books of Qur’anic commentary; their complete wording is not established as an authentic Prophetic hadith. They illustrate an opponent turning a warning of punishment into an occasion for joking and challenge. The Qur’an corrects his premise: these keepers are angels, not men of Quraysh whose strength he can calculate against his own men.
A Word from a Friend Changed a Man's Position

Ibn Ishaq’s Seerah tells of two close friends, ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, both known for intense hostility toward the Prophet ﷺ. According to the report, ‘Uqbah once sat and listened to him. Ubayy became angry on hearing this and pressured ‘Uqbah to reject the Prophet publicly, also urging him to commit a deeply insulting and harmful act against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn Ishaq connects this account to the following verses:

On that Day, the wrongdoer will bite his hands saying, “Would that I had taken a way with the Messenger!
Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!
He led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me.” Satan always betrays man.
— Qur’an 25:27–29 — Rowwad Translation Center

A close friend here means an intimate companion. The connection to these two men comes from Seerah and commentary reports, not an authentic hadith restricting the verses to them. Their meaning is broader. Nevertheless, the account illustrates another pressure in Makkah: a person could hear the Prophet ﷺ, only for friends or family to make their continued relationship conditional on rejecting what he had heard. Friendship itself could become a means of turning someone away from the truth.
A Decayed Bone in the Hand of a Man Who Denied Resurrection
One of the matters most disputed by the polytheists was resurrection after death.
How could a human being return after becoming dust and bones?

Reports in Qur’anic commentary describe a man of Quraysh coming to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, with an old, decayed bone. He crumbled it in his hand and asked, in denial, who could bring it back to life after it had decayed.
The report is narrated here in meaning, rather than as a verbatim quotation of the man’s words. Source: al-Tabari’s commentary on Qur’an 36:77, which records different accounts of his identity.
The reports differ over the man’s identity, naming either Ubayy ibn Khalaf or al-‘As ibn Wa’il. They do not establish one agreed name. The Qur’an answers the objection itself:

Does man not see that We have created him from a sperm-drop, then he becomes a clear adversary,
producing arguments against Us while forgetting his own creation. He says, “Who can give life to the bones after they have crumbled to dust?”
Say, “The One Who created them in the first place will give life to them, for He has full knowledge of every created being;
the One Who made for you fire out of the green tree, with which you kindle your fires.”
— Qur’an 36:77–80 — Rowwad Translation Center

The bones are described as worn and crumbling. Rather than beginning with how every particle will be gathered, the answer returns to the first question: who created the human being in the first place? The One who brought him into existence is not incapable of restoring him after death. The Qur’an thus preserves the very kind of objection made to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Khabbab Asks for the Wages Owed to Him

Another incident is established through an authentic chain. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him, was a blacksmith who made tools and swords. Al-‘As ibn Wa’il owed him payment for his work, so Khabbab went to collect it.

Al-‘As refused to pay unless Khabbab rejected Muhammad ﷺ. Khabbab refused and affirmed, in the meaning of the hadith, that he would not reject him even if al-‘As died and was raised again. He meant that he would never abandon his faith, not that his resolve would end at some future time.
Al-'As then took the idea of resurrection, which he mocked, and said:
“Will I be resurrected after my death?”
“If so, I shall pay you (there) if I should find wealth and children.”
Then Allah revealed:

Have you seen the one who rejects Our verses and says, “I will surely be given wealth and children [if I am resurrected]”?
Has he obtained knowledge of the unseen, or has he taken a pledge with the Most Compassionate?
Never! We will write down what he says and will prolong his punishment extensively.
We will inherit what he boasts of, and he will come to Us all alone.
— Qur’an 19:77–80 — Rowwad Translation Center
Sahih al-Bukhari 4734–4735. The two excerpts from al-'As's reply are from the English translation of hadith 4735 published by Sunnah.com.

Khabbab himself narrated the event in an authentic hadith establishing its connection to these verses. His account shows how the Qur’an was part of the Seerah: a Muslim asked for his wages, the debtor refused because of his faith and mocked resurrection, and revelation preserved and answered the objection. An argument between two men in Makkah became part of the Qur’an recited until the Day of Resurrection.
The disbelievers say about the believers, “If this [faith] were something good, they would not have believed in it before us.”
Some leading men of Quraysh went beyond refusing to sit with vulnerable believers: they treated those believers’ earlier acceptance of Islam as an argument against it. Allah says:

The disbelievers say about the believers, “If this [faith] were something good, they would not have believed in it before us.”
— Qur’an 46:11 — Rowwad Translation Center (excerpt)
They treated social status as a measure of truth, assuming that a truly good religion would have attracted people of their standing first.

Books of tafsir transmit reports connecting this meaning to some of the vulnerable believers, including Zinnirah, may Allah be pleased with her, whom we previously encountered among the women who were harmed and then freed by Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-Suyuti cites this account of Zinnirah from Ibn al-Mundhir on the authority of ‘Awn ibn Abi Shaddad; he does not present it here as a statement of the Prophet ﷺ. It is therefore cited as an exegetical report, without restricting the verse’s meaning to Zinnirah alone.

This meaning answers the elite’s objection to an enslaved person, a poor person, or a vulnerable woman recognizing the truth before them. The Qur’an rejects that measure. Truth does not become true because a wealthy person recognizes it first, nor false because a vulnerable person does.
At Other Times, the Connection Was Understood from Context

Not every connection between the Qur’an and the Seerah comes from a report identifying a particular occasion of revelation. Al-Tabari, a major Qur’anic commentator, sometimes interpreted verses in light of the Prophet’s circumstances in Makkah, showing how the accounts of earlier prophets reassured him. One example is Allah’s statement about Yusuf, peace be upon him:

When he reached his prime, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. This is how We reward those who do good.
— Qur’an 12:22 — Rowwad Translation Center
The verse speaks directly of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Al-Tabari also understood reassurance for Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in its closing words:
This is how We reward those who do good.

Just as Allah saved Yusuf after his trials and granted him authority after vulnerability, the harm faced by Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Makkah did not mean that his mission would end in hardship. This is an interpretation al-Tabari drew from the verse, not a report identifying its occasion of revelation.
Likewise, when mentioning Nuh, peace be upon him, and the long period of his call to his people, Allah says:

We sent Noah to his people, and he lived among them for a thousand years, less fifty. Then the Flood overtook them, while they persisted in wrongdoing.
— Qur’an 29:14 — Rowwad Translation Center

Al-Tabari likewise understood the account of Nuh as reassurance amid the Prophet’s suffering: prolonged resistance and harm to him and his Companions had precedents among earlier messengers, and truth ultimately prevailed. The Makkan Qur’an was not a set of commands detached from life. The accounts of earlier prophets showed the believers that others had already travelled this difficult path.
The Qur'an Reveals the Scale of the Confrontation

Reading only the historical reports may leave us with a handful of names—Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and al-‘As ibn Wa’il—and the general knowledge that they opposed the Prophet ﷺ.

Reading the verses and commentary reports alongside those events reveals the forms that opposition took: mocking punishment, denying resurrection while holding a crumbling bone, pressuring a friend to reject the Prophet ﷺ, withholding a Muslim worker’s wages because of his faith, and demanding that Bilal, Khabbab, Suhayb, and other vulnerable believers be excluded from the Prophet’s gathering.

In response, the Qur’an strengthened the believers, defended the dignity of the vulnerable, answered mockery, exposed arrogant assumptions, and taught the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that continued rejection did not prove his mission had failed. Revelation and the Seerah were closely connected: the Qur’an guided believers through events in Makkah, and its words became part of the confrontation itself.

Studying the Makkan years therefore involves two questions: what happened to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, and what was Allah revealing as they lived through those events? Answering both helps us understand the period through the first generation’s experience.
Primary Sources for This Chapter

• Tafsir al-Tabari: connections between Qur’anic verses and events of the Makkan period, distinguishing transmitted reports about occasions of revelation from interpretation inferred from context.
• Surat al-'Ankabut 29:1-3, and what al-Tabari transmitted linking them to the torture of some believers, including 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him.
• Surat al-An'am 6:52 and Surat al-Kahf 18:28, concerning the dignity of vulnerable believers and the command not to remove them from the Prophet's gathering.
• Surat al-Muddaththir 74:30-31, and reports in tafsir about Abu Jahl mocking the number of the keepers of the Fire; this account is cited as a tafsir report, without treating it as an authenticated Prophetic hadith.
• Surat al-Furqan 25:27-29, and Ibn Ishaq's connection of the verses to the story of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt and Ubayy ibn Khalaf; this is a Seerah report, not an authentic Prophetic hadith.
• Surat Ya-Sin 36:78-79; reports of tafsir differ over the identity of the man who brought the decayed bone, naming either Ubayy ibn Khalaf or al-'As ibn Wa'il, so no single name is stated as certain.
• The report of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-'As ibn Wa'il, and the revelation of Surat Maryam 19:77-80: Sahih al-Bukhari 4734-4735.
• Surat al-Ahqaf 46:11, and reports in some works of tafsir connecting its meaning to vulnerable believers, including Zinnirah, may Allah be pleased with her.
• Surat Yusuf 12:22 and Surat al-'Ankabut 29:14, and al-Tabari's method of connecting stories of earlier prophets to strengthening the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, during the Makkan period by interpretive inference, not as occasions of revelation.
• Historical report locations: al-Tabari’s commentary on 74:30–31 and 36:77; Ibn Hisham’s Seerah, the section on Ubayy ibn Khalaf, ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt, and the revelation concerning them, in the Islamweb library.
• Precise locations: al-Tabari on 29:3 for ‘Ammar, and on 6:52 and 18:28 for the accounts about sitting with vulnerable believers; Sahih Muslim 2413a for Sa‘d’s account of the six Companions. Zinnirah: al-Suyuti, al-Durr al-Manthur, 13/322, citing Ibn al-Mundhir from ‘Awn ibn Abi Shaddad. Al-Tabari’s interpretations of the stories of Yusuf and Nuh appear in his commentary on 12:22 and 29:14.

Studying the Makkan years therefore involves two questions: what happened to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, and what was Allah revealing as they lived through those events? Answering both helps us understand the period through the first generation’s experience.
Primary Sources for This Chapter

• Tafsir al-Tabari: connections between Qur’anic verses and events of the Makkan period, distinguishing transmitted reports about occasions of revelation from interpretation inferred from context.
• Surat al-'Ankabut 29:1-3, and what al-Tabari transmitted linking them to the torture of some believers, including 'Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him.
• Surat al-An'am 6:52 and Surat al-Kahf 18:28, concerning the dignity of vulnerable believers and the command not to remove them from the Prophet's gathering.
• Surat al-Muddaththir 74:30-31, and reports in tafsir about Abu Jahl mocking the number of the keepers of the Fire; this account is cited as a tafsir report, without treating it as an authenticated Prophetic hadith.
• Surat al-Furqan 25:27-29, and Ibn Ishaq's connection of the verses to the story of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt and Ubayy ibn Khalaf; this is a Seerah report, not an authentic Prophetic hadith.
• Surat Ya-Sin 36:78-79; reports of tafsir differ over the identity of the man who brought the decayed bone, naming either Ubayy ibn Khalaf or al-'As ibn Wa'il, so no single name is stated as certain.
• The report of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-'As ibn Wa'il, and the revelation of Surat Maryam 19:77-80: Sahih al-Bukhari 4734-4735.
• Surat al-Ahqaf 46:11, and reports in some works of tafsir connecting its meaning to vulnerable believers, including Zinnirah, may Allah be pleased with her.
• Surat Yusuf 12:22 and Surat al-'Ankabut 29:14, and al-Tabari's method of connecting stories of earlier prophets to strengthening the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, during the Makkan period by interpretive inference, not as occasions of revelation.
• Historical report locations: al-Tabari’s commentary on 74:30–31 and 36:77; Ibn Hisham’s Seerah, the section on Ubayy ibn Khalaf, ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt, and the revelation concerning them, in the Islamweb library.
• Precise locations: al-Tabari on 29:3 for ‘Ammar, and on 6:52 and 18:28 for the accounts about sitting with vulnerable believers; Sahih Muslim 2413a for Sa‘d’s account of the six Companions. Zinnirah: al-Suyuti, al-Durr al-Manthur, 13/322, citing Ibn al-Mundhir from ‘Awn ibn Abi Shaddad. Al-Tabari’s interpretations of the stories of Yusuf and Nuh appear in his commentary on 12:22 and 29:14.
